analysis.one_liner: Closes four tax loopholes used by the biggest oil companies and spends the revenue on highway and transit grants.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a House vote; it was referred to two committees and one subcommittee in February 2021 and died when the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would raise money for roads and transit by taking away four special tax deductions and credits that only the largest integrated oil companies use: a foreign tax credit for payments to foreign governments, immediate write-offs of drilling costs, the percentage depletion allowance, and a deduction for chemicals injected into old wells. It would also tighten the definition of a major oil company so corporate spin-offs and successors cannot escape the rules. All of the new revenue would go into a fund for the existing federal surface transportation block grant program, which states use for highway, bridge, and transit projects.
analysis.who_benefits: States and localities that build roads, bridges, and transit get new grant money, and the drivers, transit riders, and freight movers who use that infrastructure benefit. Honest taxpayers and smaller oil companies that never qualified for these preferences benefit from a slightly more level tax code.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Drivers, transit riders, and state highway programs

how_it_helps.text: The bill ends the foreign tax credit for major integrated oil companies on payments to foreign countries that are not generally applicable income taxes, a preference that lets companies count royalty-like payments as income taxes paid abroad.

It bars the largest oil companies from immediately deducting intangible drilling and development costs, requiring them instead to spread the write-off over five years, while leaving the deduction intact for smaller producers.
It sets the percentage depletion allowance for oil and gas wells to zero for major integrated oil companies, removing a deduction that lets producers shelter a fixed percentage of gross well income.
It ends the deduction for qualified tertiary injectant expenses for those companies, converting it to a five-year amortization schedule.

It closes a definitional loophole by counting any successor in interest that controls more than 50 percent of a covered company's crude oil or natural gas production as a major integrated oil company, so restructuring cannot dodge the rules.
All revenue raised by the bill would be appropriated to a new Transportation Block Grant Fund and spent on grants under the surface transportation block grant program.

analysis.who_pays: Major integrated oil companies — the small set of large firms that control most American crude and gas production — would pay billions more in federal taxes by losing these four preferences. A portion of that cost could be passed through to consumers in fuel prices.

drawbacks.text: The bill targets only major integrated oil companies; smaller independent producers keep all four tax preferences, so the burden falls on a narrow group and fuel-price pass-through would be borne by consumers if the companies raise prices.

Transportation funding is tied directly to the revenue the oil tax changes raise, so grant levels would rise and fall with the tax payments of a handful of oil companies rather than with infrastructure needs.
Restricting drilling-cost deductions and the depletion allowance for large companies could modestly discourage drilling activity by the affected firms.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit is real but modest: the revenue goes to a proven, existing grant program, and closing preferences available only to a handful of the largest companies barely dents their competitiveness against smaller rivals. The main costs are possible fuel-price pass-through and grant funding that varies with oil-company tax payments rather than with need. On balance a reasonable trade, but not transformative either for infrastructure or for oil-company taxation.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Ways and Means and Transportation committees the day it was introduced; a subcommittee referral followed two days later, neither committee ever acted on it, and it died when the two-year Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Julia Brownley introduced the bill on February 25, 2021, and it was referred the same day to the House Ways and Means Committee and the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee.

On February 26, 2021, it was referred to the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee's Subcommittee on Highways and Transit, and no further action of any kind was recorded for the rest of the Congress.
The bill drew a single cosponsor, one House Democrat, and never reached the House floor for a vote before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The major integrated oil companies are better off: they kept all four tax preferences and the revenue they generate was never redirected to transportation grants. No one else gains from the bill's death.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Big oil companies keeping their tax deductions

for.name: Rep. Julia Brownley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to close oil-company tax loopholes and route the revenue to surface transportation grants.

for.name: 1 of 213 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican joined.

against.name: Rep. Richard Neal
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: His committee received the referral on the day of introduction and never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill, whose core is tax law, was never reported out.

against.name: Rep. Peter DeFazio
against.role: Chair, House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
against.what_they_did: His committee referred the bill to the Subcommittee on Highways and Transit, which took no action for the remainder of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held, so the partisan split was never tested; the only recorded support was the Democratic sponsor and one Democratic cosponsor, with no Republican cosponsors.

industries.note: The bill strips four tax preferences available only to this handful of firms, and the transportation grant fund is financed directly by the taxes they would pay. Their interest was in keeping the deductions; the public's benefit came from taking them away.
New federal block grants would flow to state and local road, bridge, and transit projects, creating work and better infrastructure for the people who use it.

industries.industry: Small independent oil and gas producers
industries.note: All four tax restrictions apply only to major integrated companies, so smaller producers keep their deductions and drilling-cost write-offs, gaining a relative tax advantage over their largest competitors.
